full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN. This changes the first pass's label in the direction of "more known".** This isn't a variant of the Drossel–Schwabl forest-fire model. It is the Drossel–Schwabl model as it is usually written, and the 8-neighbour version is a common textbook and teaching version.

**Same rules, step for step**
- Wikipedia's definition has the same four rules, applied all at once: a burning cell turns into an empty cell; a tree will burn if at least one neighbor is burning; a tree ignites with probability f even if no neighbor is burning; an empty space fills with a tree with probability p.
- Updating every cell at the same time is part of the standard definition, not a twist. One source describes the model as updated synchronously according to the following four rules. Another says all sites are updated in parallel.
- The 8-neighbour rule is documented too. A well-known tutorial says a cell occupied by a tree becomes a burning cell if any of its eight neighbouring cells are burning. Rosetta Code's standard task asks people to implement the Drossel and Schwabl definition. Its reference code checks all 8 neighbours and uses p = 0.01, the same growth rate as yours.

**Is the behaviour documented?**
- **Bursty activity (activity_cv = 6.0):** this is the model's defining feature, fires of very different sizes. When fires are rare and fast compared with growth, the forest organises itself into a critical state without any tuning. Fire sizes then follow a power law.
- **Cells cycling through states:** each cell goes empty → tree → burning → empty. That loop is built into the rules, so scoring above chance is expected.
- **Many domains and long correlation length:** the standard picture is that the fire will spread, destroying trees in large patches. Simultaneously, in the event of a fire, new trees will grow up again. That leaves patches of trees of similar age. The spiral fire fronts you get when burning lasts a finite time (the Bak–Chen–Tang 1990 regime) are also classic results. I'm citing those from memory; I didn't open those papers in this search.

**Regime caveat (doesn't change the verdict)**
- Your p/f ratio is 100 on a 64×64 grid, and fire spreads one step at a time. That is not the critical limit. As one source notes, the model can become critical only in the limit p→0 and f→0. So expect a broad, cut-off spread of fire sizes and spreading fire fronts, not a clean power law.
- This matches the "stepwise" version, where trees regrow next to fires that are still burning, which breaks the time-scale separation the critical behaviour depends on. That is documented behaviour too.

**Genuine pattern or artefact?** Genuine. Activity is bursty, not stuck at a fixed level. Regrowth means no state can freeze permanently, and with only three discrete states nothing can blow up numerically. The fire fronts and age patches are real self-organised structure, not random colouring.
